Acts 10:28 — "And he said unto them, Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation; but God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean." (King James Version). Acts 10:14 — "But Peter said, Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean." (King James Version). Acts 10:34-35 — "Then Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons: But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him." (King James Version). Acts 11:1-18 — "And the apostles and brethren that were in Judaea heard that the Gentiles had also received the word of God. And when Peter was come up to Jerusalem, they that were of the circumcision contended with him, Saying, Thou wentest in to men uncircumcised, and didst eat with them. But Peter rehearsed the matter from the beginning, and expounded it by order unto them, saying, I was in the city of Joppa praying: and in a trance I saw a vision, A certain vessel descend, as it had been a great sheet, let down from heaven by four corners; and it came even to me: Upon the which when I had fastened mine eyes, I considered, and saw fourfooted beasts of the earth, and wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air. And I heard a voice saying unto me, Arise, Peter; slay and eat. But I said, Not so, Lord: for nothing common or unclean hath at any time entered into my mouth. But the voice answered me again from heaven, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common. And this was done three times: and all were drawn up again into heaven. And, behold, immediately there were three men already come unto the house where I was, sent from Caesarea unto me. And the Spirit bade me go with them, nothing doubting. Moreover these six brethren accompanied me, and we entered into the man's house: And he shewed us how he had seen an angel in his house, which stood and said unto him, Send men to Joppa, and call for Simon, whose surname is Peter; Who shall tell thee words, whereby thou and all thy house shall be saved. And as I began to speak, the Holy Ghost fell on them, as on us at the beginning. Then remembered I the word of the Lord, how that he said, John indeed baptized with water; but ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost. Forasmuch then as God gave them the like gift as he did unto us, who believed on the Lord Jesus Christ; what was I, that I could withstand God? When they heard these things, they held their peace, and glorified God, saying, Then hath God also to the Gentiles granted repentance unto life." (King James Version). Taken together, Acts 10:28, Acts 10:14, Acts 10:34-35 and Acts 11:1-18 give this answer; no single verse alone was treated as the full picture. These passages together, not any single verse in isolation, establish this answer.

phase1b.reply: The Israelites are the descendants of Jacob, who was also known as Israel. They are associated with the twelve tribes that descended from his sons. In the Bible, they are God's chosen people, called to live in accordance with His laws and to be a light to the nations. The story of their formation and covenant with God is a central theme throughout the Old Testament, starting from the patriarchs, particularly Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The term 'Israelites' is often used in the context of their journey from slavery in Egypt, their time in the wilderness, and their eventual settlement in the Promised Land, as outlined in books like Exodus and Joshua. The Israelites are considered foundational to the Jewish faith and identity today. Scripture does not state that directly.

phase1b.reply: Christians celebrate Sunday as a day of worship because it is believed to be the day of Jesus Christ's resurrection. While early Christians initially gathered on both the Sabbath (Saturday) and Sunday, Emperor Constantine established Sunday as a day of rest in AD 321. This was later reinforced by church councils, which encouraged Christians to honor Sunday as the Lord's Day. Over time, this practice became the norm in much of Western Christianity, though it was not mandated by explicit biblical command to replace the Sabbath. For example, in the early church, believers gathered for fellowship and worship on the first day of the week (Acts 20:7). However, the transition to Sunday observance was influenced by both civil and ecclesiastical authority rather than directly by Scripture. In summary, while the resurrection of Christ on Sunday is a key reason for its observance, historical developments played a significant role in establishing Sunday as the primary day of Christian worship.

phase1b.reply: To forgive someone, you can start by recognizing the hurt and choosing to release that burden. Jesus teaches us about forgiveness in Matthew 6:14-15, where He says, "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses." This emphasizes the importance of forgiving others as a reflection of the forgiveness we receive from God. Additionally, Ephesians 4:32 encourages us to be kind and forgiving, stating, "And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you." This reminds us that our forgiveness should mirror God's mercy towards us. As you think about this process, consider praying for the strength to forgive and for the person who hurt you, asking God to help you heal and let go of any resentment.

phase1b.message: How do faith and works work together?
phase1b.reply: Faith and works are interconnected in the life of a believer. Scripture teaches that faith is the foundation for salvation, and genuine faith naturally produces good works as a response to that salvation. For instance, James 2:17 states, "Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone." This emphasizes that true faith will manifest itself through actions. Additionally, Ephesians 2:8-10 explains that we are saved by grace through faith, and then we are created for good works: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them." Thus, works are not a means to earn salvation but rather a result of a living faith in Christ.

I'm depressed.

This reminds us that God is close to those who are hurting. He sees your pain and wants to help you through it. sabbath_depth.message: Why do many Christians observe different holidays today?
sabbath_depth.reply: Many Christians observe different holidays today due to historical developments and varying interpretations of Scripture and tradition. After the early church began to spread, different cultural influences and regional practices shaped how holidays were celebrated. For instance, the establishment of Easter and Christmas arose from a desire to celebrate critical events in the life of Jesus while also accommodating local customs. Ultimately, traditions evolved over time, leading to a diversity of observances within Christianity. Additionally, many holidays, such as Easter, are not explicitly commanded in Scripture but are based on historical events and have been adopted by various Christian denominations. This has led to differences in observance and emphasis on particular holidays across different faith communities.

critical.reply: Christians celebrate Sunday, often referred to as the 'Lord's Day,' in remembrance of the resurrection of Jesus Christ, which occurred on the first day of the week. Early Christians began gathering on this day for worship and fellowship. This practice became more formalized over time, especially after Emperor Constantine, in AD 321, declared Sunday a day of rest across the Roman Empire, aligning with the growing Christian community. The Council of Laodicea around AD 364 encouraged Christians to honor this day, which led to its establishment as a normal day of worship in much of Western Christianity. It's important to note that this transition did not come from an explicit biblical command to change the Sabbath from Saturday to Sunday, but rather from historical developments and church authority over time.

critical.message: What happened to Jerusalem under Rome?
critical.reply: In AD 70, Jerusalem faced a devastating siege led by Roman forces under General Titus. The city was captured, and the Second Temple was destroyed, marking a significant turning point in Jewish history. This destruction ended the Temple-based sacrificial system that had been central to Jewish worship. Josephus, a Jewish historian who witnessed these events, documented this destruction in his work, *The Wars of the Jews*. This event fulfilled Jesus' prophecy about the Temple's destruction, as noted in Matthew 24:1-2, where He tells His disciples that not one stone would be left upon another. The fall of Jerusalem led to the scattering of many Jewish people and marked the beginning of a new phase in the relationship between Rome and the Jewish population, as well as the early Christians who were also affected by these events.
